message:
feat(update): the installer is part of the package it installs

GNLinkSetup.exe is what Add/Remove Programs runs, and until now an update left
it behind. Its uninstall path is bound to compile-time constants -- the payload
list, the service name, the folder name, the shortcut names -- so a build that
renamed or removed a file would leave the old uninstaller unable to clean up
after it. It now travels in the package and goes through the same staging,
backup, replacement and rollback as every product file. Not copied afterwards:
a copy that does not participate in rollback can leave a new uninstaller beside
old binaries, which is worse than the situation it was meant to fix.

What this does not do, and should not be described as doing: it brings the
maintenance code up to the current version, and nothing more. Files removed or
renamed by earlier builds, and leftovers from a service that has since changed,
are not cleaned up by it. Any such cleanup belongs to explicit install
ownership with a rollback plan, never to a sweep of the install folder.

The version check is a consistency check between two things that should agree,
not proof of identity. GNLinkSetup.exe carries no VERSIONINFO resource, so the
same UTF-16 string scan the project already uses for release verification asks
whether the staged artifact mentions the version the manifest claims. Finding
it does not establish that the binary IS that version -- the manifest's hash is
what pins which bytes arrived. What it catches is a manifest paired with the
wrong artifact.

The updater refusing to replace itself is now checked rather than assumed. It
lives outside the install directory by design, but a mistaken config could name
its own image among the payload and the swap would move the running executable
aside, so validate() looks.

A running GNLinkSetup.exe now counts as a product process. If one is up an
uninstall may be in progress, and swapping its binary underneath that is worse
than not updating. The name only finds candidates; identity still decides.

Three regressions, all against real OS behaviour: a hash that does not match
leaves both the old Setup and the old product files untouched; a locked Setup
fails the swap without leaving the product file replaced; and a failure after
the swap rolls back the old Setup along with everything else.

One limit that cannot be engineered away: until a first update arrives, the
0.2.104 Setup already installed governs uninstalling, and it cannot be reached.

Still missing: there is no multi-file package format yet. The staged artifact
is a single file that Swap copies to each payload name, which is a test
simplification, not a shipping design.

qwinsta: console active, rdp-tcp listening. 126 checks here, 526 across the
eight suites; the installer relinks clean and the three live PIDs are unchanged.
